conditions.unmeasured: figures downstream of a constant nobody has measured are absent rather than estimated
conditions.what_an_interval_here_is: a statement about this model's declared inputs, and nothing about whether the model has the right structure (ch14, ch19)

produced_by.sampler: sizing.mc — inverse transform, Iman-Conover rank correlation

summary.description: A TCO built by the seller of a system, not by its buyer. The seller cannot see the customer's workload or its bill, so the model starts from the customer's spend per host and scales it three ways: by how many hosts the customer runs, by the share of that spend that moves with the number of hosts, and by the product's benchmark advantage, discounted for how much of it carries over to this customer's work. It is top down and linear in hosts. It has no measured constant and no ceiling, so it is a definitional model: what a seller can honestly build before a customer opens their books (ch23).

benchmark_advantage.label: benchmark advantage per host
benchmark_advantage.note: One number: the vendor publishes one figure, and a range here would put words in its mouth. The doubt about it lives in the transfer factor.

provenance.source: The seller's own benchmark: how much more work one proposed host did than one of the customer's current hosts, on the benchmark's workload. Here it is the ratio of the two hosts' cores in ch22 (sixty-four against sixteen), standing in for a published result.

break_even_transfer.label: transfer factor at which the saving is zero
break_even_transfer.note: A break-even only while the part of the spend that scales is larger than the cost of the move. Below that no transfer factor pays, and the figure is negative.

break_even_usage.label: hosts at which the saving is zero
break_even_usage.note: A break-even only while the margin per host-year is positive. Otherwise no usage pays, and the figure is negative.

current_cost_per_host.label: customer's spend per host-year, everything in

provenance.source: What the seller supposes a customer spends a year for each host it runs, staff included: the whole bill divided by the hosts. Lognormal, because a spend cannot be zero or less and its high side runs further than its low. The customer knows this figure; the seller does not.

current_per_year.label: customer's spend a year, as it is

current_total.label: customer's spend over the horizon, as it is

provenance.source: The web service model's horizon (ch02), the refresh cycle the fleet is bought against

margin_per_host_year.label: saving per current host-year, before the move
margin_per_host_year.note: What each host the customer runs today saves a year, before the move is paid for. If it is zero or less, no amount of usage pays for the move.

move_cost.label: cost of the move
move_cost.note: One number: ch22's estimate of the move, held as ch22 holds it, so the two chapters price the same move.

provenance.source: The challenger's migration cost in ch22: the one-off cost of moving to the proposed system

payback.label: years until the move is paid back
payback.note: A break-even in time: the year in which the savings add up to the cost of the move. Only a payback while the saving a year is positive; otherwise the move is never paid back, and the figure is negative.

proposed_cost_per_host.label: proposed spend per host-year, staff and move excluded
proposed_cost_per_host.note: One number: the seller's own price, which it states as one figure.

provenance.source: The seller's price for running one proposed host for a year: the host spread over the horizon, its licence, support and power, and no staff. Here it is the challenger's quote in ch22, worked out per host-year; tests/the_sellers_tco and bench/run_seller.py check it against the stamped result.

proposed_hosts.label: proposed hosts, capacity-equivalent
proposed_hosts.note: Not rounded up. A top-down model counts capacity, not boxes, and rounding here would make the break-evens approximate instead of exact.

proposed_per_year.label: customer's spend a year, with the product

proposed_total.formula: current_total * (1 - scaling_share) + proposed_hosts * proposed_cost_per_host * horizon + move_cost
proposed_total.label: customer's spend over the horizon, with the product

saving_per_year.label: saving a year, before the move

scaling_share.label: share of the spend that moves with hosts

provenance.source: How much of that spend goes away when a host does. Hardware, power, licences and support move with the host count; staff and anything bought per site largely do not. A brochure that scales the whole bill has set this to one without saying so. Triangular, because it is a lowest, most likely and highest guess, and a share has hard ends.

transfer_factor.label: share of the benchmark advantage that carries over

provenance.source: How much of the benchmark's advantage survives on this customer's work rather than on the benchmark's. Nobody has measured it for any customer: that would take running the customer's own workload on both hosts. One means the benchmark is the customer's workload. Triangular, because it is a lowest, most likely and highest guess, and a seller who claimed a more precise shape would be inventing it.

usage_hosts.label: hosts the customer runs today
usage_hosts.note: One number: a count, which the customer can give the seller by asking. The chapter's answer about customer size is the break-even usage below, and a band here would only blur it.

provenance.source: The seller's picture of a customer in its market, not a count of any one customer's hosts. The customer can replace it with a count, and then it is the customer's figure, not the seller's.

scenario.because: The two figures a seller can learn by asking, pinned to ch22's incumbent: the hosts it runs and what it spends per host-year, everything in, at the point estimates. The share that scales and the transfer factor stay the seller's guesses, so the result can be set beside ch22's bottom-up comparison of the same customer.
